sections.title: What monetary policy is and who runs it

blocks.text: **Monetary policy** is the way a central bank uses the tools it controls (interest rates, reserve ratios, liquidity operations) to reach the goals laid down in its law. In India the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** is given this job, and the duty is written into the **RBI Act, 1934**. Money and credit are steered by the central bank, while taxes and spending (fiscal policy) belong to the Government.

blocks.title: Core ideas
rows: The Reserve Bank of India, under a mandate in the RBI Act, 1934.
Maintain **price stability** while keeping the objective of growth in mind.
It is a necessary precondition for sustainable growth.
A mix of **direct** and **indirect** tools: policy rates, reserve ratios, liquidity operations.

blocks.title: Coins versus notes
blocks.text: Do not credit the RBI with everything about currency. Coins of all denominations are minted by the **Government of India**; the RBI handles the issue of notes and conducts monetary policy.

sections.title: Repo, reverse repo, MSF and Bank Rate

blocks.text: These four rates are the RBI's price signals to banks. Three of them sit inside the **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF)** and the fourth is a penal borrowing window. Think of them as a ladder: banks borrow from the RBI at the upper rungs and park spare money with the RBI at the bottom.

blocks.title: The policy rates
rows: The **fixed** interest rate at which the RBI gives overnight money to banks against the collateral of government and other approved securities, under the LAF.

The **fixed** interest rate at which the RBI absorbs surplus money from banks overnight against eligible government securities, under the LAF. The RBI also holds variable-rate reverse repo auctions when market conditions need them.

Scheduled commercial banks can borrow **extra** overnight money from the RBI by dipping into their SLR portfolio, up to a limit, at a **penal** rate. It is a safety valve against sudden liquidity shocks.
The MSF rate and the reverse repo rate form the corridor within which the weighted average call money rate moves day to day.

The rate at which the RBI is ready to buy or rediscount bills of exchange and other commercial paper. It is published under **Section 49** of the RBI Act, 1934, and is aligned to the MSF rate, so it moves automatically when the MSF rate moves with the repo rate.

blocks.title: The rate corridor (high to low)
items: Penal window; top of the corridor
RBI absorbs liquidity; bottom of corridor

blocks.title: Repo or reverse repo?
blocks.phrase: REPO: banks REnt money from RBI. REVERSE repo: banks REturn (park) money with RBI.
letters: RBI lends -> liquidity goes INTO the banking system -> banks pay the repo rate
RBI borrows -> liquidity is SUCKED OUT of the system -> banks earn the reverse repo rate
blocks.note: Always read it from the RBI's side: in a reverse repo the central bank is the borrower.

blocks.title: Order of the rates
blocks.phrase: Penal pair on the roof, Repo on the middle floor, Reverse repo in the basement.
letters: MSF rate and Bank Rate (highest, penal)
blocks.note: MSF and Bank Rate are aligned; the corridor is bounded by MSF above and reverse repo below.

sections.title: Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio

blocks.text: Both ratios are fixed as a percentage of a bank's **Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)**, which is roughly its deposits and similar liabilities. They decide how much of the money a bank collects is locked away and how much is left to lend.

blocks.title: CRR versus SLR
rows: Safe and liquid assets: unencumbered government securities, cash and gold
A per cent of NDTL notified by the RBI from time to time in the Gazette of India
Changes how much cash banks can use for lending
Changes the resources available for lending to the private sector

blocks.title: CRR or SLR?
blocks.phrase: C for Cash and RBI. S for Securities and Self (the bank itself).
letters: Cash Reserve Ratio: cash balance kept with the RBI
Statutory Liquidity Ratio: liquid assets (G-secs, cash, gold) kept by the bank itself

blocks.title: Cut and effect
blocks.text: If the RBI **lowers** the CRR, banks have more money to lend and credit creation **increases**. If it raises the CRR, lending capacity shrinks. The same logic applies to the SLR.

sections.title: LAF, OMO and MSS: managing liquidity

blocks.title: Liquidity operations
rows: Made up of overnight and **term repo auctions**. The RBI has progressively increased the share of liquidity injected through fine-tuning variable-rate repo auctions of different tenors.
To help develop the inter-bank term money market, which can then set market-based benchmarks for pricing loans and deposits and so improve the transmission of monetary policy.
Outright **purchase and sale of government securities**: a purchase injects durable liquidity and a sale absorbs it.
Introduced in **2004**. Surplus liquidity of a lasting nature (from large capital inflows) is absorbed by selling short-dated government securities and treasury bills.

blocks.title: How the MSS mops up surplus cash
Durable or daily?
blocks.text: LAF (repo and reverse repo) handles **day-to-day** liquidity. OMOs and MSS handle **durable or enduring** liquidity. Link: OMO = buy or sell G-secs; MSS = sell short-dated G-secs and T-bills.

Central bank tools are usually grouped by what they act on. **Quantitative (general) tools** change the total amount or cost of credit in the whole economy. **Qualitative (selective) tools** steer credit toward or away from particular uses. Exams usually ask you to spot which group a tool belongs to.

blocks.title: Two families of tools
rows: Overall volume and cost of credit
Bank Rate, repo and reverse repo, CRR, SLR, open market operations
Direction of credit to specific uses
Margin requirements, credit rationing, moral suasion, direct action, regulation of consumer credit

blocks.title: What raising or cutting does
items: Higher repo rate or CRR: credit becomes costlier or scarcer, which helps cool demand and inflation.
Lower repo rate or CRR: money becomes cheaper and more plentiful, which supports growth.
Market-determined variables such as the inflation rate are outcomes, not tools; the RBI does not fix them.

blocks.title: How the framework arrived
items: Government and RBI sign an **Agreement on Monetary Policy Framework** that starts flexible inflation targeting.
The **RBI Act, 1934 is amended** to give inflation targeting a statutory basis.
The first target period begins: **4 per cent CPI inflation**.
End of the first target period (5 Aug 2016 to 31 Mar 2021).

blocks.title: The target and its limits
rows: The **Government of India**, in consultation with the RBI, **once every five years**.
**Consumer Price Index (CPI)** inflation, notified at **4 per cent** for the first period.
Upper limit **6 per cent**, lower limit **2 per cent**.
Average inflation stays **above the upper limit** or **below the lower limit** for **three consecutive quarters**.
The weighted average call rate (WACR), kept at or around the policy repo rate through daily liquidity management.

blocks.title: How a repo rate change reaches inflation
items: Anchored at or near the repo rate
Key driver of inflation and growth

blocks.title: The 4-plus-or-minus-2 band
blocks.phrase: Four is the aim, two and six are the fence; three quarters outside the fence means the target has failed.
letters: Lower and upper tolerance limits (4 minus 2, 4 plus 2)
Consecutive quarters outside the band = failure
Years between target reviews by the Government
blocks.note: As per the 2024-25 syllabus. The Government reviews the target every five years, so check the latest notification for the current period.

blocks.text: Before the 2016 amendment the framework rested only on the 2015 Agreement. The amended Act gives the RBI an explicit **legislative mandate** to run the framework: set the policy repo rate after assessing the present and expected macro situation, and adjust liquidity to keep money-market rates close to it.

The **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** decides the policy interest rate needed to achieve the inflation target. **Section 45ZB** of the amended RBI Act provides for an empowered **six-member** committee, which the **Central Government** constitutes by notification in the Official Gazette.

blocks.title: Who sits on the MPC
rows: Deputy Governor in charge of Monetary Policy
One RBI officer nominated by the RBI Central Board
Appointed by the Central Government; hold office for **four years** or until further orders, whichever is earlier

blocks.title: Members named in the book (at the time of writing)
rows: Ashima Goyal, Shashanka Bhide and Jayanth Varma

blocks.title: Inside three, outside three
blocks.phrase: Three RBI insiders (Governor, Deputy Governor, one officer) plus three outsiders make six; outsiders serve four years.
letters: Governor, Deputy Governor for monetary policy, one RBI officer (all ex officio)
Members 4, 5 and 6 appointed by the Central Government
blocks.note: Names change as terms end, so learn the structure rather than the people.

blocks.title: Six, not nine
blocks.text: The MPC is a **six-member** committee. A statement calling it a nine-member committee is wrong. The Central Government, not the RBI, constitutes it.

blocks.title: From analysis to announcement
items: The RBI's **Monetary Policy Department (MPD)** assists the MPC; stakeholder views and the RBI's analytical work feed the repo rate decision.
The MPC meets **at least four times a year**; the **quorum is four** members.
Each member has **one vote**. If votes are tied, the **Governor has a second (casting) vote**.
After every meeting the **resolution** is published, as required by Chapter III F of the RBI Act, 1934.
On the **14th day** the **minutes** are published: the resolution, each member's vote and each member's statement.

The **Financial Markets Operations Department** carries out the policy through daily liquidity operations, and the **Financial Markets Committee** meets daily to keep the operating target close to the repo rate.

blocks.title: Supporting bodies and documents
rows: Assists the MPC in formulating monetary policy.
Operationalises policy mainly through day-to-day liquidity management.
Meets daily to review liquidity conditions so that the operating target stays near the policy repo rate.
Published **once every six months**; explains the sources of inflation and gives a **6 to 18 month** inflation forecast.
Older advisory panel of experts (monetary economics, central banking, markets, public finance); its role was only advisory and it **ceased to exist** once the MPC was formed.

blocks.title: The numbers of the MPC
blocks.phrase: Six members, four meetings, four for quorum, four-year terms; minutes on day 14; report every six months.
letters: Minimum meetings a year; also the quorum; also the term of external members in years
Day on which the minutes are published
Gap between Monetary Policy Reports (forecast 6 to 18 months ahead)
blocks.note: In practice the RBI holds about six policy meetings a year, but the law only requires a minimum of four.

blocks.text: At the time the source was written (April 2023), after six consecutive increases the MPC decided to **pause** the rate-hike cycle amid concerns over global financial stability and kept the **policy repo rate unchanged at 6.5 per cent**. Rates move often, so treat this as a dated reference and check the latest policy before an exam.

blocks.title: Frequent confusions
items: Repo means the RBI **lends** to banks; reverse repo means the RBI **absorbs** money from banks.
CRR is held **with the RBI** in cash; SLR is held **by the bank itself** in safe assets such as G-secs and gold.
Bank Rate is linked to the **MSF** rate, not to the reverse repo rate.
Inflation rate is **not** a tool; it is a market outcome the policy tries to influence.
The MPC has **six** members and the Governor has only a **casting** vote in a tie.

blocks.title: Dated numbers
blocks.text: Repo rate level, membership of the MPC and the inflation target period are taken as per the 2024-25 book. They change with time; the structure and rules stay the same.

revision: RBI conducts monetary policy under the RBI Act, 1934; the primary objective is price stability keeping growth in mind.
Coins are minted by the Government of India; the RBI conducts monetary policy.
Repo rate: fixed rate at which RBI lends overnight to banks against government and approved securities under LAF.
Reverse repo rate: fixed rate at which RBI absorbs liquidity from banks overnight.
MSF: extra overnight borrowing by dipping into SLR at a penal rate; MSF rate and reverse repo rate form the corridor.
Bank Rate: rediscount rate for bills, published under Section 49 of the RBI Act and aligned to the MSF rate.
CRR is the share of NDTL kept as cash with the RBI; SLR is the share of NDTL kept in safe liquid assets by the bank itself.
Lowering CRR increases credit creation; raising it reduces lending capacity.
OMOs are outright purchase or sale of G-secs; MSS (2004) absorbs durable surplus liquidity through T-bills and short G-secs.
Inflation target: 4 per cent CPI with a band of 2 to 6 per cent; set by the Government with the RBI every five years.
Target fails if inflation is outside the band for three consecutive quarters.
Flexible inflation targeting got a statutory basis through the May 2016 amendment; earlier it rested on the Feb 2015 Agreement.
MPC (Section 45ZB): six members, constituted by the Central Government; Governor chairs and has a casting vote.
MPC meets at least four times a year, quorum four; minutes come on the 14th day; Monetary Policy Report every six months.
April 2023: MPC paused after six hikes and kept the repo rate at 6.5 per cent (dated figure).
